title: Episode 112: John Adams and the Boston Massacre: The Courage of the Defense
description:
In 1770, following the bloody Boston Massacre, young attorney John Adams risked his political career, his legal practice, and his family's safety to defend the hated British redcoats in court, proving that the rule of law must prevail over mob rule.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the tense, riot-torn streets of Boston, Massachusetts, on the snowy night of March fifth, seventeen seventy, to witness one of the most heroic acts of moral courage in legal history: John Adams's defense of the British soldiers in the Boston Massacre. When British redcoats opened fire on an unruly mob on King Street, killing five colonists, the entire province erupted into a fury for blood. The soldiers and their captain faced certain hanging at the hands of an enraged public. Every prominent lawyer in Boston refused to represent them—except thirty-four-year-old John Adams, a fiery Son of Liberty who despised British taxation, yet revered the rule of law above life itself. In the face of death threats, vandalized property, and the wrath of his own cousin Samuel Adams, John Adams stood alone before a hostile jury to proclaim that 'Facts are stubborn things.' Here is George with the full, gripping story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: AN OCCUPIED CITY ON THE EDGE
In the late seventeen sixties, the seaport city of Boston, Massachusetts, was a simmering cauldron of political acrimony, economic grievance, and military tension. Enraged by the Townshend Acts, which levied parliamentary taxes on imported glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea without colonial consent, Bostonians had staged boycotts and violent riots that terrified royal customs commissioners. In October seventeen sixty-eight, the British Crown dispatched four thousand red-coated soldiers of the Fourteenth and Twenty-Ninth Regiments to occupy the town of sixteen thousand citizens.
For eighteen grueling months, Boston lived under military occupation. British sentries challenged citizens on street corners, military fife and drum corps paraded through the streets on the Sabbath, and off-duty redcoats competed with local laborers for scarce dockyard jobs at cut-rate wages. Fights and brawls erupted daily in taverns and along the waterfront ropewalks between foul-mouthed soldiers and young apprentices armed with wooden clubs.
Observing the escalating crisis was thirty-four-year-old attorney John Adams. Born in Braintree, Adams was a Harvard-educated country lawyer with an incandescent intellect, an unbending moral compass, and a deep reverence for English common law. While John was an ardent Son of Liberty who penned blistering essays against parliamentary taxation, he viewed street mobs and riots with profound aristocratic revulsion, believing that genuine liberty could only survive within the strict guardrails of constitutional order. Tavern arguments frequently escalated into brawls as dockworkers and ropemakers clashed with British soldiers moonlighting for subsistence wages.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BLOODSHED ON KING STREET
The inevitable explosion arrived on the bitterly cold, moonlit night of Monday, March fifth, seventeen seventy-one. Outside the Custom House on King Street—modern-day State Street—Private Hugh White of the Twenty-Ninth Regiment stood solitary guard at his sentry box. A young wigmaker's apprentice began taunting a passing British officer over an alleged unpaid bill, and Private White stepped in to defend his officer, striking the boy with the butt of his musket.
Shouting for help, the boy drew a crowd. Church bells—normally rung only for fires—began to toll wildly across the town, drawing hundreds of agitated men and boys into the snowy streets armed with heavy clubs, walking sticks, and chunks of firewood. Within minutes, an angry, screaming mob of over three hundred men surrounded Private White's sentry box, pelting him with iceballs, oyster shells, and sharp rocks, shouting: 'Kill him! Kill the damn lobster-back!'
Terrified, White retreated up the stone steps of the Custom House, cocking his musket and shouting for the main guard. Captain Thomas Preston marched out of the guardhouse with six grenadiers and a corporal, pushing their way through the surging crowd with fixed bayonets to form a defensive semi-circle around the sentry box. The crowd pressed within inches of the bayonet tips, striking the soldiers' muskets with clubs and daring them to pull the trigger: 'Fire, damn you, fire if you dare!' Private White endured a barrage of insults, sharp rocks, and frozen snowballs from the surging mob, knowing that drawing his sword meant court-martial.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FATAL VOLLEY AND THE KNOCK ON ADAMS'S DOOR
Suddenly, out of the darkness, a heavy wooden club struck Private Hugh Montgomery, knocking him flat onto the icy cobblestones. Montgomery lost his musket in the fall; rising in panic amidst the roaring mob, he retrieved his weapon and discharged it into the crowd. Seconds later, amidst chaotic shouts and flying debris, the other soldiers fired their weapons in an irregular, ragged volley.
When the acrid white sulfur smoke cleared over King Street, five Bostonians lay dead or dying in the stained snow: Crispus Attucks, a courageous sailor of mixed African and Indigenous heritage who was struck twice in the chest; Samuel Gray; James Caldwell; seventeen-year-old Samuel Maverick; and Patrick Carr. Six others were wounded. The town was on the brink of armed insurrection. Royal Governor Thomas Hutchinson was forced to stand on the balcony of the Old State House and promise the furious crowd that the soldiers would be arrested and tried for murder according to the law.
The following morning, Captain Thomas Preston and his eight soldiers were locked in the stone cells of the Queen Street jail. Every prominent attorney in Boston refused to represent the redcoats, fearing the wrath of the mob and the destruction of their practices. At dusk, a frantic Tory merchant named James Forrest knocked on the door of John Adams's modest home, with tears streaming down his cheeks, begging Adams to take the defense. Without hesitation, Adams accepted, demanding only a modest retainer of one guinea, stating firmly that counsel ought to be the very last thing an accused man should want in a free country. The tragic death of Crispus Attucks on the King Street cobblestones became an immediate rallying symbol of patriotic resistance throughout New England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TRIAL OF CAPTAIN PRESTON
John Adams's decision to defend the soldiers detonated a political firestorm across Boston. Friends and clients crossed the street to avoid speaking to him, hostile crowds yelled insults outside his front door, and prominent Sons of Liberty, led by his own radical second cousin Samuel Adams, denounced him for providing legal cover to royal butchers. Yet Adams remained completely unyielding, joined in the defense by young Josiah Quincy Jr. and Robert Auchmuty.
Recognizing that passions were at a fever pitch, Adams strategically maneuvered to delay the trials for seven months until autumn seventeen seventy, allowing the public fury to cool. In late October, the first trial commenced in the Queen Street courthouse: the trial of Captain Thomas Preston, who faced execution on charges of murder for allegedly ordering his men to fire.
In a brilliant cross-examination of prosecution witnesses, Adams exposed fatal contradictions in the eyewitness testimony. Witnesses admitted that in the deafening uproar of church bells and roaring crowds shouting 'Fire!', it was impossible to distinguish whether the word 'Fire!' had come from Captain Preston or from the rioters who were daring the soldiers to shoot. Adams proved that Preston was standing in front of his men, between their bayonets and the mob, where ordering a volley would have resulted in his own death. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty, acquitting Captain Preston of all charges. Adams meticulously demonstrated to the court that popular hysteria could not be permitted to replace empirical evidence in a capital trial.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TRIAL OF THE EIGHT SOLDIERS
A month later, on November twenty-seventh, seventeen seventy, the supreme legal drama commenced: the trial of the eight enlisted soldiers of the Twenty-Ninth Regiment. The prosecution, led by Robert Treat Paine and Samuel Quincy, presented dozens of witnesses portraying the soldiers as bloodthirsty mercenaries who had fired on peaceful citizens without provocation.
John Adams's defense strategy was grounded in the fundamental common law right of self-defense. Adams took an extraordinary, high-risk tactical gamble: rather than seeking sympathy from a Boston jury, he went out of county to ensure an impartial jury composed entirely of rural farmers from outside Boston who had not experienced the military occupation. Adams then presented detailed, visceral testimony reconstructing the terrifying violence of the mob on King Street.
Witnesses described how the crowd had hurled chunks of ice, oyster shells, and spiked clubs, and how Private Montgomery had been knocked down and struck with clubs. Medical testimony from the deathbed of Patrick Carr was introduced: the dying Irish immigrant had confessed to his doctor that the soldiers had been provoked beyond human endurance and had fired purely in self-defense to save their own lives. Adams had turned the prosecution's narrative on its head. The defense called over thirty witnesses to reconstruct the terrifying violence of the crowd, establishing that the soldiers fired in self-defense.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: 'FACTS ARE STUBBORN THINGS'
On December fourth, seventeen seventy, John Adams rose before the crowded courtroom to deliver his final closing argument: one of the greatest orations in the history of Anglo-American jurisprudence. Speaking for hours by the flickering light of tallow candles, Adams articulated the supreme philosophy of the rule of law over popular passion.
Adams thundered to the jury: 'I will enlarge no more on the evidence, but submit it to you, gentlemen, facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictums of our passions, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence. Nor is the law less stable than the fact; if an assault was made to endanger their lives, the law is clear, they had a right to kill in their own defense.'
He continued with a magnificent defense of individual liberty against state oppression: 'The law, in all vicissitudes of government, fluctuations of the passions, or flights of enthusiasm, is obstinate, inflexible, impassionate. If the law will not allow that to be justifiable, it will allow it to be excused. It were better that ten suspected witches should escape, than that one innocent person should be condemned. For the law holds that it is more good that eight guilty persons should escape unpunished, than one innocent person should suffer.' Adams's immortal defense of the rule of law elevated the Boston trials into a landmark triumph of Anglo-American constitutional justice.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT AND THE TORCH OF JUSTICE
On December fifth, seventeen seventy, the jury returned its verdict. To the astonishment of Boston and the entire British Empire, six of the eight soldiers were found completely not guilty and acquitted of all charges. The remaining two soldiers, Private Hugh Montgomery and Private Matthew Kilroy, were found not guilty of murder, but convicted of manslaughter for having discharged their weapons without direct physical danger.
Under ancient English common law, Montgomery and Kilroy pleaded the 'benefit of clergy'—a medieval legal privilege that allowed first-time offenders to escape execution. In open court, the two soldiers were branded with the letter 'M' on the brawn of their right thumbs with a hot iron to signify manslaughter, and discharged from the army to return to England. The legal ordeal was over.
John Adams's defense of the British soldiers was a monumental triumph for the moral foundation of the American Revolution. In an era when political trials in Europe regularly resulted in state-sponsored lynchings, Adams and a colonial Boston jury proved to the world that the American cause was founded not upon lawless mob rule, but upon the sacred, unwavering supremacy of the rule of law.
Years later, looking back upon his long, illustrious career as diplomat, Founding Father, and second President of the United States, John Adams wrote in his diary: 'The part I took in defense of Captain Preston and the Soldiers, procured me anxiety and obloquy enough. It was, however, one of the most gallant, generous, manly, and disinterested actions of my whole life, and one of the best pieces of service I ever rendered my country.' It remains the eternal standard of legal integrity in a free society. The acquittal of the British soldiers proved to the world that the American cause was founded upon principle rather than vengeance.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
John Adams later described his defense of the British soldiers as one of the best pieces of service he ever rendered his country. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we witness Adams as President during the Quasi-War, standing alone against his own cabinet to keep America out of war with revolutionary France.
